sections.heading: Priority List PR Overview
sections.summary: Jannik opened a PR to Lucid adding a priority-list mechanism for trusted key publishers, replacing the earlier whitelist concept.
sections.body:
- Jannik posted a [PR to the Lucid EIP](https://github.com/shutter-network/EIPs/pull/1/changes) roughly 30 minutes before the call; participants had not yet reviewed it in depth.
- The PR splits into two parts:
  - An EL voting contract that lets validators vote on key publishers, with results propagated to the CL as a priority list.
  - Changes to Lucid's block-ordering rules on the CL to interpret and enforce the priority list.
- A queuing mechanism was added to decouple contract changes from CL execution, limiting the rate of changes and preventing spam; modeled on similar patterns in validator consolidation EIPs.
- A fee mechanism was added to further discourage spam, also borrowed from existing EIP patterns.
- Key messages now require a signature from the key publisher to prevent impersonation — without this, anyone could claim their transaction's key came from a prioritized publisher and gain top-of-block placement.
  - Signing key messages was preferred over signing tickets, as it is operationally simpler for key publishers who already perform key releases.
- Max preceding commitments were removed because combining them with the priority list ordering is complex; the priority list is seen as a cleaner replacement.
  - Lucid's recovery mechanism (for missed or invalid payloads) was extended to reorder transactions that violate priority-list ordering, which would have made max preceding commitments difficult for key publishers to predict.
- Justin described the removal of max preceding commitments as "aesthetically pleasing" and clearer than the previous mechanism.
- Engine API changes are still needed to communicate the priority list between EL and CL; Jannik has not yet drafted these.
- Action items:
  - Justin to review the full PR (targeting same day) and specifically examine Engine API implications.
  - Justin to get review attention from Ander and Julian (Lucid authors).
  - Justin to escalate to Tama, who had concerns about optionality in the design.
  - Justin to add Jannik to the Lucid authors list if this contribution is pulled in.

sections.heading: Voter Set for the Priority List
sections.summary: The current proposal uses all active validators weighted by effective balance; a smaller subset may suffice but is not yet proven necessary.
sections.body:
- The voting body in the proposal is the full set of active validators, weighted by effective balance.
- Justin suggested restricting the voter set, e.g. to validators that already have duties in the epoch; Jannik agreed a smaller subset would likely suffice but doubted it would simplify things.
- The tally is computed iteratively so contract-level changes do not require full recomputation, but effective-balance changes (once per epoch) do force a recalculation.
- Preliminary benchmarks from Jannik look acceptable for the full validator set.
- Justin suggested consulting CL client teams on whether restricting the voter set would improve efficiency enough to justify the change.

sections.heading: Key Validation and Publisher Accountability
sections.summary: There is no automatic mechanism to penalize key publishers for invalid reveals; the validator set must vote them out manually or via external monitoring.
sections.body:
- Justin raised the question of how invalid key reveals (wrong key vs. no key at all) feed back into the priority list.
- Lucid already rejects invalid keys, and the PR adds an additional rejection condition for invalid signatures, but neither triggers automatic removal from the priority list.
- A misbehaving key publisher remains in the priority section (bottom of top-of-block at worst) until validators vote them out.
- Jannik proposed that external monitoring software could track key publisher behavior and guide validator voting decisions.
  - The same tooling could also document a path for new key publishers to join: start working outside the priority section, build a track record, and eventually be voted in.
- No decision was made on adding automated punishment; the design currently relies on social/governance-layer enforcement.

sections.heading: Top-of-Block Fee Retention
sections.summary: The top-of-block fee will be kept to regulate congestion within the priority section; ordering by key-publisher trust was rejected to avoid collusion.
sections.body:
- Jannik initially suggested the top-of-block fee could be removed since the priority list already handles ordering, but Justin pointed out it is still needed to regulate who gets into the size-constrained priority section during congestion.
- Within the priority section, transactions are ordered by top-of-block fee regardless of which key publisher was used, as long as the publisher meets the 50% vote threshold.
- Transactions from different key publishers can be interleaved — the priority section is a set of all transactions meeting the trust threshold, not grouped by publisher.
- Ordering by key-publisher trust level was explicitly rejected: MEV searchers should not compete on key trust, as this could create strange collusion dynamics.
- Agreement: keep the top-of-block fee as the ordering dimension within the priority section.

sections.heading: Key Message Signing Format
sections.summary: The key message signing format awkwardly mixes RLP and SSZ conventions because key publishers use EL addresses, not BLS keys; better formulations are sought.
sections.body:
- Jannik flagged that the key message signing in the PR is syntactically unsatisfying: it combines RLP transaction signing with SSZ container signing.
- CL container signing normally uses BLS signatures, but key publishers are identified by execution-layer addresses, so an EL signing scheme is required instead; which one was left open.
- Frame transactions were briefly considered as an abstraction layer, but key messages are not transactions — they are consensus-layer messages that happen to use the EL signing scheme.
- Justin noted a potential interaction with frames if key-origin validation were treated as a frame within a transaction, but this was not developed further.
- No resolution; better ways to express the signing format are an open item for reviewers.

sections.heading: Action Items and Wrap-Up
sections.summary: Participants are asked to review the PR, share it with CL client teams, and provide feedback before the next call.
sections.body:
- Homework for all attendees: read the PR, leave comments, and run it by their local CL developers.
- Call ended at approximately the 30-minute mark, returning 30 minutes to participants.
